title: Idempotency, retries and timeouts
subtitle: Why one retry can charge a customer twice, and the small key that stops it.

c.v: Priya is on a train with weak mobile data. She taps
in a shopping app. The request reaches the payment server, and the server charges her card.
The answer back to her phone is lost. After 10 seconds the app hits its
timeout
. It keeps the spinner on and sends the same request again: an automatic
retry
The server sees a new request and charges the card again. Priya now has two charges of ₹1,499. Support spends a day finding and refunding the double charges.
A retry is safe only if doing something twice has the same effect as doing it once. That property has a name:
idempotent
Reading a balance is idempotent. "Set the order status to shipped" is idempotent. "Charge ₹1,499" is
not
: each call takes more money.
The key idea.
A timeout tells you that you did not get an answer. It does not tell you that the work did not happen.
So we make the charge idempotent. The app creates one unique
idempotency key
for the payment and sends it with every attempt. The server remembers each key and its result. If the same key comes again, the server sends back the saved result instead of charging again.
Step through what happens when the answer is lost. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.

Two details matter in real systems. If a second request with the same key arrives while the first is still running, the server must not start a second charge. Stripe's v1 API does not run it or save a result for it, and the app can retry later. And if the same key arrives with a different amount, the server should reject it: that is a bug in the app.
Never retry
Nothing runs twice.
Users see more failed payments.
A person can easily check and try again.
Retry, no key
It can charge twice.
Cheap to build.
The call is already idempotent, like a read or "set status to shipped".
Retry with an idempotency key
Repeats get the saved result.
You store keys, handle "still running", and delete old keys.
Payments, orders, anything that creates something.
Key + backoff with jitter
And retries are spread out.
One user may wait a little longer.
Many clients may retry at the same moment, for example after an outage.
Simple rule:
add a key to every call that creates or moves something. When you retry, add
backoff
with
jitter
, so retries do not hit a struggling service at the same moment. Also limit the number of retries.

sections.name: At work
sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: In design reviews, ask:
"What happens if this call runs twice?"
Ask it for every call that creates something or moves money.
Put a timeout on every network call. A call without one can wait forever and hold a thread or a connection.
Retry in one layer only. If the app, the gateway and the service each try 3 times, one tap can become 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 calls.
Wait longer between tries with exponential backoff and jitter, so clients don't all retry in the same second.
Keep keys long enough to cover every retry. Stripe's v1 API, for example, keeps them for at least 24 hours.
"Add an Idempotency-Key header to the create-payment call. Create the key once per payment, before the retry loop."
"Write a test where the first response is lost and the client retries with the same key. Assert that the card is charged exactly once."
The key is made
outside
the retry loop, not inside it.
The server saves the key and the payment in the same database
transaction
A second request with the same key, while the first still runs, does not charge again.
Retries happen in one layer, with a limit and backoff.
Keys belong to one customer, so nobody can read another person's result.

q.v: The app's Pay request times out. What do you know for sure?

options.v: Nothing. The server may or may not have charged the card.

why.v: A timeout only means no answer came back in time. The work may have happened.

q.v: When should the app create the idempotency key?

options.v: Once per payment, before the first try.
The server creates it after charging.

why.v: Every retry must carry the same key, or the server can't tell it is a repeat.

q.v: The app, the gateway and the payment service each make up to 3 attempts in total. How many charge calls can reach the bank from one tap?

why.v: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27. Retries multiply across layers, so retry in one layer only.
